growth_story.headline: UK income per person has grown slowly since the 2008 crisis, held back by weak productivity and investment, then by the pandemic and an energy shock.
growth_story.arc: The data show one long era since 1990: income per person grew 1.4 percent a year on average over 1990–2025, with no lasting shift of 2 points or more. Inside that era the pace slowed after the 2008 financial crisis: income per person fell 5.3 percent in 2009, and growth averaged 0.5 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 0.8 percent over 2016–2025. The IMF and the OECD trace the slowdown to a sharp fall in productivity growth after the crisis, and to weak business investment, whose recovery stalled after the 2016 Brexit referendum. The pandemic cut income per person by 10.2 percent in 2020, followed by rebounds of 8.2 percent in 2021 and 4.1 percent in 2022. Then high energy prices, made worse by Russia's war against Ukraine, squeezed household incomes: income per person fell 1.0 percent in 2023 and was flat in 2024. Growth returned to 1.1 percent in 2025, when income per person reached its highest level yet, though only about where it first stood in 2018.

threads.title: Productivity slowdown after 2008
threads.text: Since the 2008 financial crisis, output per worker has grown much more slowly than before. The IMF still describes weak productivity as the main obstacle to growth and living standards, and links it to low investment and low private research spending.

threads.text: Business investment was already weak, and its recovery stalled after the 2016 referendum to leave the EU. The OECD says policy uncertainty has weighed on business investment, and in 2024 the IMF noted that firms trading with the EU were still adapting to the new arrangements.

threads.text: The pandemic brought the deepest fall in income per person in the series, in 2020. After a quick rebound, high energy prices made worse by Russia's war against Ukraine fed a cost-of-living crisis and activity stalled in 2023, before inflation fell back as energy prices eased.

threads.title: More workers, not more output
threads.text: Between 2010 and 2019, growth came mostly from more people working, not from higher output per worker. Since the pandemic, more people have dropped out of the workforce because of long-term illness, which higher migration has only partly offset.

growth_story.tension: The sources date a sharp productivity slowdown to the 2008 crisis, but the data find no lasting break since 1990, because the drop in income-per-person growth (to 0.5 percent over 2006–2015 and 0.8 percent over 2016–2025) stays below the tool's 2-point threshold. The IMF also described a soft landing after a mild recession in 2023 and growth at its potential rate in 2025, while income per person fell 1.0 percent in 2023, was flat in 2024 and grew 1.1 percent in 2025. Part of that gap is a growing population: the whole economy grew faster than income per person, and the IMF notes higher migration numbers.
